Three separate choices determine a result:

1. **The physical model:** what is grounded, the outer boundary, the size of
   the vacuum and substrate, junction values, and material properties.
2. **The metal representation:** how the metal is turned into geometry for the
   solver.
3. **The numerical settings:** mesh, element order, adaptive refinement and
   solver tolerances.

Refining the mesh improves the solution *of one model*. Changing a boundary or
a junction value creates *a different model*. Keep the two kinds of study
separate when you compare results.

## The physical model

Record, for every result: which conductors are grounded, the outer boundary
condition, the extent of the substrate and vacuum, any ports or junctions and
their values, and the material properties used.

The default outer boundary differs between solvers. A Palace Eigenmode model
with no boundary assigned uses a perfect magnetic conductor (PMC). HFSS
Eigenmode uses a perfect electric conductor (Perfect E). The same geometry
therefore gives different frequencies in the two solvers.

## Metal representation in Palace

Palace offers two representations, called **Route A** and **Route B**:

| Route | Metal is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A | A zero-thickness PEC sheet | Needs a thin-film profile: `substrate_face` keeps the real face position; `metal_gap_equivalent` adjusts it to match the gap |
| B (default) | A finite-thickness solid with a PEC surface | The metal interior is not meshed |

Both treat the metal as a perfect conductor; neither models conductor loss.
Switching route changes the model; it is not a way to fix a difficult mesh.
See the [geometry reference](../geometry-sgb.qmd) for details.

HFSS and Q3D have a similar choice, `modeling="solid"` or `"thin_film"`; see
[Solid and thin-film modeling](../specs/aedt-runtime.qmd#aedt-solid-thin-film).

## Numerical settings

| Setting | Controls |
|---|---|
| Mesh size | Element size near and far from the metal |
| Geometry order (`geometry_order`) | How closely elements follow curved surfaces |
| Element order (`order`) | Accuracy of the field approximation within each element |
| Adaptive refinement (`amr_max_passes`, `amr_tolerance`) | How many times, and until what error estimate, the mesh is refined |
| Solver tolerance | When the linear or eigenvalue solver stops |

Geometry order and element order are independent. Palace's `HighOrderOutput`
only affects how output files are written.

### Judging convergence

A solver's "converged" flag means its own stopping rule was met. It does not
mean the quantity you need is accurate. Look at the history of that quantity
across refinement passes:

- An eigenvalue residual and an adaptive-mesh error estimate measure different
  things.
- A frequency can settle while a surface participation is still changing.
  Check the quantity you use, not a different one.

The Palace mesh summary reports element counts and an *estimate* of the
number of unknowns; it is not a convergence measure. The mesh-quality report
evaluates straight-sided tetrahedra and does not assess curved elements.

For surface EPR near curved edges, see the
[curved inset reference](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#curved-positive-inset-distance).

## What is unknown stays unknown

Some quantities are not computed: HFSS does not compute film energy on metal
sidewalls, and a loss tangent you did not set is unknown. SCGSim reports these
as missing or unknown rather than zero, even when the rest of the result is
available.
